findings.title: SQL Injection via unsanitized 'id' parameter in SQLi page [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload 1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 seeded user records: (admin/admin), (Gordon/Brown), (Hack/Me), (Pablo/Picasso), (Bob/Smith). FALSE payload 1' AND '1'='2 returned zero records (page showed only 'User ID:' prompt with no ID/First name/Surname output). This confirms classic boolean-based SQL injection due to unsanitized string concatenation of the 'id' GET parameter into the backend SQL query.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via unsanitized 'ip' parameter in Ping tool [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Response pre_block contained normal ping output (4 packets transmitted/received, rtt stats) followed immediately by the literal string 'www-data' on its own line - the output of the injected 'whoami' shell command appended via the unescaped ';' command separator. This confirms the 'ip' field is passed directly to a shell command without sanitization, and the web server process runs as the 'www-data' user.

findings.title: Stored Cross-Site Scripting via unsanitized guestbook 'mtxMessage' field [security=low]
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ (session=dvwa_admin) form_data={txtName: 'tester', mtxMessage: '<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'} -- note: client-side maxlength=50 was bypassed by submitting the raw form_data directly via HTTP POST, payload serve
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] After storing the payload, re-loading the guestbook page as an authenticated user executed the injected script. browser_eval_js('window.xss_flag') returned 1 (the exact result value, not a string). browser_read_dom('#test_token') confirmed presence of the live DOM element with inner_html_excerpt 'window.xss_flag=1', proving the <script id="test_token"> tag was stored and rendered unescaped in the page HTML and executed by the browser. findings.title: Stored XSS in Guestbook Message field bypasses medium-level filter (DVWA xss_s) [security=medium]
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/  (session=dvwa_admin) -> confirmed page banner 'Security Level: medium'

POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ (session=dvwa_admin) form_data={txtName: 'tester2', mtxMessage: '<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'} -> HTTP 200, guestbook entry stored
GET/browser_navigate http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ (session=dvwa_admin) -> page reloaded, rendered comment list includes the new entry

browser_eval_js("JSON.stringify(Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('script')).map(s=>({id:s.id, text:s.textContent})))") -> confirms a live <script id="test_token"> element with textContent 'window.xss_flag=1' exists in the rendered DOM
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] DVWA's medium-level stored-XSS filter for the mtxMessage field performs a plain, exact, case-sensitive str_replace('<script>','') (non-recursive, no regex/attribute handling). Our canary payload `<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>` does NOT contain the literal bare substring "<script>" (it contains "<script id=\"test_token\">" instead), so the filter's exact-match replace does not strip it and the full script element is stored and reflected verbatim into the guestbook HTML. After submitting via POST and reloading the page in an authenticated browser context, document.querySelectorAll('script') shows a live element with id="test_token" and textContent "window.xss_flag=1" injected into the page, and browser_eval_js('window.xss_flag') returned 1, proving the injected script executed in the victim's browser context. This is a confirmed stored XSS bypass of the medium-level sanitizer (attribute-bearing script tags evade the naive exact-string filter).

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) via /rest/basket/{id}
findings.response_evidence:
Step 1 (acct1, own_basket_id=6): 200 OK, body: {"status":"success","data":{"id":6,"UserId":22,"Products":[{"id":1,"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)", ... "BasketItem":{"ProductId":1,"BasketId":6,"id":9,"quantity":3}}]}} — confirms acct1's own seeded basket (id=6, UserId=22) contains Apple Juice (1000ml) qty=3.

Step 2 (acct2, own_basket_id reported separately as 7, but request targets acct1's basket id=6): 200 OK, IDENTICAL body returned: {"status":"success","data":{"id":6,"UserId":22,"Products":[{"id":1,"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)", ... findings.title: Confidential Acquisitions Memo Exposed via Open Directory Listing /ftp/
findings.response_evidence:
Step 1: 200 OK, serve-index directory listing rendered for unauthenticated user, listing includes link and size for 'acquisitions.md 909' among other sensitive files (announcement_encrypted.md, coupons_2013.md.bak, incident-support.kdbx, package.json.bak, suspicious_errors.yml).

Step 2: 200 OK, content-type text/markdown, body retrieved without authentication:
"# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year.
This will have a significant stock market impact as we will elaborate in detail in the following paragraph: ... Our shareholders will be excited. It's true. No fake news."
This confirms the open directory listing exposes and allows retrieval of a confidential internal acquisitions memo (CWE-200).

findings.title: Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection in /rest/user/login (email field)
findings.response_evidence: Response: HTTP 200, body: {"authentication":{"token":"<JWT present>","bid":1,"umail":"admin@juice-sh.op"}}. The injected email `' OR 1=1--` short-circuits the SQL WHERE clause (comment truncates the password check), causing the login query to match the first user record in the table and return a valid signed authentication token along with umail="admin@juice-sh.op" and bid=1 (the admin's basket id), despite supplying an arbitrary/invalid password ("anything"). This confirms successful authentication bypass for the admin account via SQL injection (CWE-89). (No credentials for admin@juice-sh.op were known/used — the only input was the malicious email string.)

findings.title: Product-Search SQL Injection via unsanitized 'q' parameter
findings.response_evidence: Request 1 (single quote) returned HTTP 500 with body: "Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \"'%'\": syntax error" - proving the raw input is concatenated unsanitized into a backend SQL query (classic SQLi error signature). Request 2 (9-column UNION injection) returned HTTP 200 with a well-formed JSON response: {"status":"success","data":[{"id":1,"name":2,"description":3,"price":4,"deluxePrice":5,"image":6,"createdAt":7,"updatedAt":8,"deletedAt":9}]} - the literal integers 1-9 supplied in the UNION SELECT were reflected directly as field values in the product object, proving the injected UNION query was executed successfully by the backend and its column count/structure was inferred correctly. This combination (syntax-breaking error + successful UNION result reflecting attacker-controlled literals) is conclusive proof of exploitable SQL injection.

findings.title: Unauthenticated exposure of user feedback records containing PII (email addresses)
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/api/Feedbacks (no Authorization header, unauth session)
findings.response_evidence: Request made with zero authentication headers/cookies returned HTTP 200 with a JSON array of 8 feedback records. Each record associated with a registered user (UserId 1, 2, 3, 21) includes a 'comment' field embedding a partially-masked but still disclosed email address fragment tied to the real account, e.g.: UserId 1 -> "I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)"; UserId 2 -> "Great shop! Awesome service! (***@juice-sh.op)"; UserId 3 -> "Nothing useful available here! (***der@juice-sh.op)"; UserId 21 -> comment containing a BIP39-style seed phrase AND email fragment "(***ereum@juice-sh.op)". The records also leak internal UserId linkage mapping feedback to specific user accounts, and the seed-phrase content in UserId 21's comment is itself sensitive PII-adjacent data. No authentication was required to access any of this, confirming unauthenticated PII/sensitive-data exposure via CWE-359.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal bypasses file-extension filter on /ftp/ to retrieve restricted .bak file
findings.response_evidence: Request 1 (direct restricted file) returned HTTP 403 with body: "Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!" thrown from verify() in fileServer.js:55, confirming the extension allow-list filter blocks direct .bak access. Request 2, appending a URL-encoded null byte followed by an allowed extension (package.json.bak%2500.md), returned HTTP 200 with content_type application/octet-stream and the FULL verbatim content of the restricted package.json file (not package.json.bak%2500.md), including: {"name": "juice-shop", "version": "6.2.0-SNAPSHOT", "description": "An intentionally insecure JavaScript Web Application", ... "dependencies": {...sqlite3, sequelize, jsonwebtoken...}}. This proves the filename-suffix check against ".md"/".pdf" passed (since the string ends in .md), while the underlying filesystem read truncated the path at the null byte and actually opened/served "package.json.bak", confirming a classic poison null-byte path traversal / filter bypass vulnerability (CWE-22).

findings.title: Exposed Encryption-Keys Directory Listing (/encryptionkeys/)
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 with content_type text/html; serve-index directory listing rendered. visible_text: 'listing directory /encryptionkeys/ ~ / encryptionkeys / Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM'. Links enumerated: http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub and http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/premium.key — both sensitive key files exposed to unauthenticated directory browsing, satisfying CWE-548 criteria (browsable listing + exposure of premium.key and jwt.pub).
